pageTexts.5:
Executive summary

The assessment identified behavioral health, including mental health and substance use, as the community's most significant health need. Residents, clinicians and community partners described long waits for counseling, a shortage of providers who accept Medicaid, and rising overdose deaths in the county.

Housing instability and the cost of rent were raised in every focus group and ranked second among prioritized needs. Focus group participants connected housing to nearly every other issue raised, from missed appointments to untreated chronic conditions.

Basic needs such as food, transportation and child care were grouped as a single priority area. Residents asked that the hospital keep these issues together because the same families are affected by all of them.

pageTexts.18:
Community input: focus groups and listening sessions

Six focus groups were held between March and May 2023 with 54 participants. Several residents said they no longer feel safe walking to the clinic after dark. Others described a lack of lighting along the main road and asked for later bus service.

Families who speak Spanish described waits of several weeks for appointments with an interpreter, and some said they brought a child to translate instead.

Transportation to specialty appointments in the city remains the biggest barrier for seniors. Several participants said they had stopped seeing a specialist altogether because of the drive.

pageTexts.21:
Prioritized community health needs

The steering committee ranked needs using severity, the number of people affected, and the hospital’s ability to act. The five priorities are listed below.

Priority 1: Behavioral health, including mental health and substance use.

Priority 2: Housing and basic needs.

Priority 3: Healthy weight, nutrition and physical activity for children and adults.

Priority 4: Tobacco and vaping prevention among youth.

Priority 5: Access to care, including primary care, dental care and transportation. Access to prenatal and maternal care was listed under access to care.

pageTexts.24:
Evaluation of the 2020 implementation plan

Food security. In partnership with the Valley Food Bank, the hospital hosted a monthly produce distribution in the clinic parking lot. Over three years the distributions served about 400 households a month. The hospital's community benefit fund awarded $25,000 to the Valley Food Bank to expand weekend meal programs for students.

Immunization. Hospital staff ran drive-through flu and COVID-19 vaccine clinics on six Saturdays, giving 1,840 doses. Volunteers from the county health department staffed registration.

Workforce. The hospital expanded its nurse residency program to twelve positions, added a paid medical assistant apprenticeship with the community college, and offered tuition reimbursement to forty employees pursuing clinical degrees, with the goal of filling vacancies that had remained open for more than a year.
pageTexts.25:
Evaluation of the 2020 implementation plan, continued

Behavioral health. The hospital and Valley Behavioral Health co-located a crisis counselor in the emergency department, supported by a hospital grant. The counselor saw 1,120 patients in the first year.

Financial assistance. Financial counselors screened every uninsured patient for charity care and enrolled 612 people in the hospital's financial assistance program. The hospital also simplified its application from six pages to two.

Coverage. Enrollment specialists helped 388 patients complete Medicaid applications at the bedside. Outreach to the outlying communities is described on the next page.
pageTexts.26:
Evaluation of the 2020 implementation plan, continued

Outreach. The mobile health unit visited the three outlying communities every other week. Visits included blood pressure checks, vaccinations and help with prescriptions.

The unit was taken out of service for four months in 2022 for repairs, and visits resumed in early 2023.

A school nurse: "Kids are coming to school hungry and anxious, and we have one counselor for 600 students."

A clinic manager in the north end: "People up the valley drive ninety minutes for a routine visit, and in winter they just don't go."

An emergency department social worker: "We see patients discharged to a tent because there is nowhere else."

Community resources: food, housing and basic needs

Valley Food Bank – weekly pantry, Tuesdays and Fridays, no ID required.

Mercy Valley Shelter – 24 beds, intake from 5 pm, call ahead in winter.

Valley Dental Van – free cleanings for children under 12, call for schedule.

County Housing Authority – rental assistance applications, first Monday of each month.

pageTexts.10:
Priority 1: Mental health and substance use

Strategy 1.1: Add two licensed counselors to the primary care clinic by 2025.

Strategy 1.2: Partner with the county crisis line to add a warm handoff from the emergency department to outpatient counseling.

Strategy 1.3: Train 200 community members in Mental Health First Aid through hospital-led classes each year.

Measures: counseling wait time under 14 days; number of warm handoffs; number trained.
pageTexts.11:
Priority 2: Basic needs and economic security

Strategy 2.1: Offer Medicaid and SNAP application help at every financial counseling visit.

Strategy 2.2: Collaborate with community partners on housing, including the regional housing coalition.

Priority 3: Access to care

Strategy 3.1: Expand the hospital's diabetes prevention and healthy weight classes to two evenings per week.

Measures: applications completed; coalition meetings attended; class enrollment.
